court: Office of Hearings and Appeals — Director's Decisions (U.S. Dept. of the Interior)
title: 39 OHA 259 — IN RE LAVADIE
text:
IN THE MATTER OF ELAINE B. LAVADIE
DIR-2009-0027 Decided October 28, 2009
Appeal from a determination made by a Board of Survey, New Mexico State
Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Santa Fe, New Mexico, finding
employee, Elaine B. Lavadie, financially liable for damages caused by her negligence
in operating a U.S. Government-owned vehicle, a 2005 Ford Explorer 4x4, vehicle
number I-421898, Report of Survey No. GDRS090001.
Reversed.
1. Property Board of Survey: Negligence: Motor Vehicle
A Report of Survey determination of employee liability in simple
negligence will be reversed when the record reflects that the
motor vehicle accident at issue was not the result of the
employee’s failure to exercise the degree of care that a prudent
person would exercise under like circumstances.
2. Property Board of Survey: Administrative Procedure: Generally:
Employee Participation
A determination of employee liability in simple negligence
will be reversed where the employee was not given an
opportunity to provide a written statement and make an
oral presentation to the Board of Survey prior to its
determination of findings.
APPEARANCES: Elaine B. Lavadie, Santa Fe, New Mexico, pro se.
39 OHA 259

DIR-2009-0027
OPINION BY CHAIRMAN BRUCE A. JOHNSON
Introduction
Elaine B. Lavadie (Appellant), an employee with the New Mexico State Office,
BLM, Santa Fe, New Mexico, has appealed the January 28, 2009, decision of the
Reviewing Official, affirming the findings and determinations of the Board of Survey
(Board), New Mexico State Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Santa Fe,
New Mexico, finding her negligent and financially liable for damage to Government-
owned property, a 2005 Ford Explorer 4x4 truck, vehicle number I-421898, arising
out of a October 5, 2007, accident at the U.S. Post Office in Santa Fe, New Mexico.
Pursuant to 410 DM 114-60.808-4, Appellant was assessed $250 in damages. The
decision was transmitted to Appellant by memorandum dated January 29, 2009,
from Gwen Rush, Property Utilization Specialist, National Business Center, BLM,
Denver, Colorado. Appellant’s appeal was received by the Office of Hearings and
Appeals on March 2, 2009, and was assigned Docket No. DIR-2009-0027. BLM
transmitted the official file to this Office on March 16, 2009. The file consists in
pertinent part of: the Report of Survey (GDRS090001), signed by the Reviewing
Official on January 28, 2009, with the attached report of the Board; an estimate for
repair from CF Collision, Santa Fe, New Mexico, in the amount of $410.29; an
estimate for repair from Crystal Clear Body Shop, Inc., Santa Fe, New Mexico, in the
amount of $369.81; and an estimate for repair from Mobile Auto Restoration Service,
Espanola, New Mexico, in the amount of $264.45. There were no photographs of the
damaged vehicle in the file.
Apparently, Appellant did not file an official accident report form, Standard
Form 91; however, in describing the accident in an “Accident Report”, she stated
that:
I drove a Government vehicle (Ford Explorer, New Mexico license
number 1421898) to the U.S. Post Office [2010 S. Pacheco, Santa Fe, NM] to
drop off the outgoing mail for the Bureau of Land Management. I dropped the
mail off at the loading dock. I had my seat belt buckled and my mirrors
adjusted; I proceeded to back-up out of the dock area. I did not back out far
enough prior to turning in order to swing out and drive forward, therefore I
bumped into a short (about 4 feet high) concrete pole (which I did not see in
the mirror or through the back window). I sustained small property damage
to the passenger side of the bumper. I came back to the office and verbally
reported the incident to Darlene Ortiz, Property Manager Specialist. I was also
going to report it to Charles Byrd, Regional Safety Officer, but he was out of
the office.
Accident Report, dated October 5, 2007.
39 OHA 260

DIR-2009-0027
There is no indication in the record that the Chairperson, Board of Survey,
New Mexico State Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Santa Fe, New
Mexico, notified Appellant that a Board of Survey was being initiated to determine
employee liability concerning her accident or that Appellant was informed of her
right to submit a written explanation of the circumstances surrounding the accident
and to make an oral presentation to the Board. There is a memorandum dated
January 16, 2009, in the file from the Board Chairperson to Appellant providing her
with the Board’s Findings and Recommendation.
The Board of Survey Decision
In its findings and determination dated January 16, 2009, the Board found
Appellant liable for “simple negligence” in the amount of $250.
In explaining its finding, the Board stated:
The Board has found the employee accountable for simple
negligence. Based on further discussion with the employee, the Board
feels if the employee would have utilized the driver/passenger side
mirrors, she would have seen the 4 ft. poles on both sides of the vehicle
and not cut her turn too short.
Board of Survey Findings, dated January 16, 2009.
By memorandum dated January 29, 2009, Gwen Rush, Property Utilization
Specialist, National Business Center, BLM, Denver, Colorado, informed Appellant that
she had been found negligent and financially liable for damage to the vehicle
resulting from her October 5, 2007, accident.
Argument on Appeal
In her appeal, received on March 2, 2009, Appellant indicates that she wishes
to contest the determination of the Board of Survey. First, Appellant argues that she
had not been given proper training in the operation of this size vehicle, stating that:
I am appealing a determination of simple negligence for the damage of
Government vehicle number 1421898. I am requesting relief from
accountability in the amount of $250....
A more fair solution would have been for the Survey Board to
recommend proper training on the operation of large Government Vehicles.
39 OHA 261

DIR-2009-0027
I have always driven small cars; this vehicle is a large Ford Explorer 4x4. I
have never had any training driving a large vehicle.
. . . .
The only reason I was driving a large vehicle was because the mail
courier service that had a contract to pickup and deliver the mail for the New
Mexico State Office closed overnight. They did not notify us (or their
employees) that they were closing. The Bureau of Land Management decided
not to pay a professional mail courier to continue courier service. The
responsibility of getting the mail to and from the post office was passed on to
the two employees sharing the duties of the mail clerk position (I was one of
them). My supervisor, at the time, suggested to me that I use my personal,
new, vehicle to run back and forth to the post office. Because the person I
shared the mail duty with took the bus to work, he would have to use my car.
I did not want the vehicle’s interior being scuffed up with the mail bins, etc.
and more important, I did not want someone else driving my car. It was then
decided that a Government Vehicle would be dedicated to us for the sole
purpose of picking up the morning mail and taking the outgoing mail in the
afternoon.
With respect to the convening of the Board of Survey, the fact that she did not
receive notice and her knowledge of the Board proceedings, Appellant stated that:
I do not think that policy (if there is a policy) regarding notification
that an employee is to appear before a Board was followed. I was not given
written notice that I was going to be called before the board. The accident
happened on October 5, 2007. It was 15 months before I was called,
without prior notice, to appear before the Board. After the Board met
regarding my case, I found out that other employees receive a memorandum
notifying them of the meeting and instructing them on what to do and when
to be there. The day I was called before the Board, I was attending
Correspondence Training - someone who knew where the training was
being held came and called me out of training to appear before the board. I
did not know I was going to testify. This was my only experience before such
a board - in fact I did not know exactly what a Board of Survey does - I do
now.
Next, Appellant provides her perspective on the findings of the Board
regarding her negligence stating that:
39 OHA 262

DIR-2009-0027
The accident happened in the afternoon when I was backing up out of
the loading dock at the U.S. Post Office; I had dropped off the outgoing mail.
My written statement said I used my mirrors, yet I was asked if I used my
mirrors, I stated that I did (but I still did not see the object I backed into - it
could have been in a blind spot). Now, upon reflection, I wonder if I was
being tricked into incriminating myself. I know that I did all the things I
should have done prior to backing up - I did not see anything in my path. No
one witnessed the accident, but I immediately reported the incident. That
should demonstrate integrity.
I was assured by the person I reported the accident to that the damage
was so minor and the vehicle was going to be excessed soon, so I should not
be overly worried. I was asked to submit a written explanation, enter the
accident online into the Safety Management Information System, and take the
vehicle for estimates. I did the first two but was never able to take time from
my duties to take the vehicle to any shops for estimates.
At the time of the accident, I had multiple duties which included:
• Staff Assistance for the Branch of Support Services;
• Quicktime lead for New Mexico/Oklahoma/Texas/Kansas; and
• Mail clerk (a temporary duty which started in April 2007). This later
became a shared position until August 18, 2008 when the other person
quit and it again became my duty.
All those positions have tight deadlines and I was never able to leave
the office to take the vehicle for estimates. During that time period, I was
many times assured not to worry about the estimates because the damage was
so small.
In December 2008 when a full time mail person was hired, the Bureau
of Land Management also hired a professional courier service; I was finally
able to take time to take the vehicle for estimates.
Appeal, dated February 26, 2009.
Review of the Survey Decision
[1] At issue in this case is whether the Board of Survey properly concluded
that the damage to the Government vehicle resulted from simple negligence on the
39 OHA 263

DIR-2009-0027
part of Appellant. Simple negligence, as defined at 410 DM 114-60.808-1(b)(2), is
“an act or omission of the employee where they failed to exercise the degree of care,
precaution, attention, and vigilance that a prudent person would exercise under like
circumstances.” Where an employee exercises the degree of care which a prudent
person would exercise under like circumstances, the fact that an accident occurs will
not render the employee liable. 410 DM 114-60.808-1(a).
It has been recognized in the general law of employee liability that an
employee has a duty to his employer to exercise a reasonable degree of care, skill,
and judgment in the performance of his duties of employment. 27 Am. Jur. 2d
Employment Relationship § 220 (1996); 30 C. J. S. Employer-Employee Relationship
§ 111 (1992). With regard to the relationship between operation of Government
vehicles and the influence of outside factors on that operation, some guidance is
provided by principles of negligence law. Courts have held that an individual’s
conduct is a legal cause of the event if it was a material element and a substantial
factor in bringing it about. 57A Am. Jur. 2d Negligence § 435 (1996). To be a
material element and a substantial factor in a negligent act, there must be some duty
violated.
The record in this case does not support the determination of simple
negligence. In its findings, the Board based its determination of simple negligence on
the conclusion that “if the employee would have utilized the driver/passenger side
mirrors, she would have seen the 4 ft. poles on both sides of the vehicle and not cut
her turn too short.” The Board’s conclusion is in direct conflict with Appellant’s
October 5, 2007, written statement which she made at the time of the accident. In
her statement, Appellant indicated that:
I dropped the mail off at the loading dock. I had my seat belt buckled
and my mirrors adjusted; I proceeded to back-up out of the dock area. I did
not back out far enough prior to turning in order to swing out and drive
forward, therefore I bumped into a short (about 4 feet high) concrete pole
(which I did not see in the mirror or through the back window).
In her appeal, Appellant states that when asked by the Board, she informed the
Board that she had used the mirrors when backing up in the vehicle, but did not see
the pole which may have been in a blind spot. Appellant states that she had also
noted this in her October 5, 2007, written statement which was made at the time of
the accident. Despite two statements by Appellant that she used the mirrors, the
Board concluded without explanation that if she had “utilized the driver/passenger
side mirrors, she would have seen the 4 ft. poles [sic] on both sides of the vehicle.”
The Board made no effort to explain its conclusion, which is not in accord with
Appellant’s statement of the facts. Despite Appellant’s statement that she did not see
the concrete pole, the Board did not indicate how it resolved this conflict. The Board
does not state that it found Appellant’s statement unbelievable, nor did the Board go
39 OHA 264

DIR-2009-0027
to the scene to view the pole and the surroundings to determine if Appellant’s version
was feasible or correct. There are no photographs of the scene, which may have
helped either to support the Board’s conclusion or Appellant’s version of the accident.
At a minimum, where there is a direct conflict between the Board’s conclusion and
Appellant’s statement of what happened, the Board should attempt to resolve the
conflict by explaining its reasoning or indicate that it does not accept Appellant’s
version, either because it is not believable or it is not supported by other evidence.
In view of the preceding, we conclude that Appellant’s version of the accident
is credible and there is nothing in the file to contradict her statement that she did not
see the pole when looking in the mirror or through the rear window. In this case, the
Board clearly did not prove negligence by Appellant in her operation of the
Government vehicle.
Therefore, we conclude that Appellant’s conduct did not constitute simple
negligence, and she is not financially liable for $250.
[2] With respect to the notice that the Board of Survey must give an employee,
the Departmental Manual provides in pertinent part that:
(a) Prior to convening a board of survey the Chairperson, Board of
Survey or Survey Officer will send written notification to the employee
who may be held liable for property loss, and afford the employee the
opportunity to present a written statement of facts surrounding the loss.
Any such statement must be presented to the Board of Survey/Survey
Officer by the employee within fourteen (14) calendar days of the date
of the notification. The statement(s) will become part of the Report of
Survey and will be considered in the investigation and determination of
financial liability.
(b) The employee may also orally address the Board within the same
time frame, but must provide an accompanying written statement of
any facts they wish the Board to include in the Report of Survey.
410 DM 114-60.808-2.
In this case, there is no evidence that Appellant was notified that she had the
opportunity to address the Board through a written statement and make an oral
presentation as provided in the Departmental Manual. In fact, Appellant states in her
appeal that she did not receive notice from the Board.
The Departmental Manual does not provide specific instructions for notifying
employees of the opportunity to present written and oral statements on their behalf.
The Departmental Manual only states that “written notification” will be sent to the
39 OHA 265

DIR-2009-0027
employee and that the employee will be afforded the opportunity to present a written
and an oral statement of the facts surrounding the property loss. 410 DM 114-
60.808-2. This lack of notice is troubling because had she been afforded the
opportunity to prepare for the Board meeting and to address the issues prior to a
decision, Appellant may have persuaded the Board, in accordance with 410 DM
§ 114-60.808-1(a), not to hold her liable, and thus obviated the need for any further
proceedings. We have held that where due process is not afforded and the employee
is not provided a fair opportunity to present evidence for the Board of Survey’s
consideration in determining its findings, the Board of Survey’s determination of
simple negligence on the part of the employee will not be affirmed on appeal. See In
re Susan LaFranchi-Madonich, 24 OHA 73 (2003); In re Don E. Skaggs, 12 OHA 106
(1996); In re David B. Luttrell, 13 OHA 176 (1996). The Board in this case did not
ensure that the Appellant was notified in accordance with the Departmental Manual.
While a lack of diligence on the part of the cognizant employee or
obstructionist tactics may justify the Board’s going forward in his/her absence, that is
not the case here. Glaring procedural inconsistencies and a lack of explanation in the
record, such as was found in this case, undermines the integrity of the Board of
Survey process and warrants reversal of the Board’s decision. See In re Loretta Park,
17 OHA 116 (1999); In re William M. Wilson, 13 OHA 156, 161 (1996); In re
Judith M. Kish, 13 OHA 185, 187-89 (1996).
The evidence shows that the Board in this case made no effort to provide the
employee with a fair review of her case before determining that she was negligent
and financially liable. The Board did not convene until 15 months after the accident,
yet there is no explanation why there was such a lengthy delay. After the 15-month
delay, the Board did not send Appellant the requisite notice that the Board would
review her case and that she could provide a written statement and appear in person
before the Board. Instead of providing the requisite notice of her opportunity to
appear, the Board orally summoned Appellant to its meeting. Without notice,
Appellant was called from a training session to appear before the Board. Without an
opportunity to prepare her points and a presentation, Appellant appeared before the
Board and according to her, she “testified”. Appellant does not indicate what she
“testified” to, nor does the Board provide an indication of the content of her
“testimony”. It is unclear why the Board thought this was appropriate, or complied
with the DM provisions regarding the review to be performed by a Board of Survey.
The fact that the Board called the employee before the Board on the day it met does
not satisfy the DM requirements. To expect the employee to leave a training session
and, without notice, appear before an investigatory body, such as the Board, is
patently unfair and contrary to Departmental requirements, and basic fairness.
Based upon the preceding, we conclude that the Board failed to provide
Appellant with the minimum notice required by the DM and did not permit her to
make a written presentation to the Board as required by the DM. Moreover, we
39 OHA 266

DIR-2009-0027
conclude that the personal appearance before the Board provided by the Board was
not in accordance with the DM requirement. Accordingly, we reverse the Board’s
decision finding Appellant negligent and financially liable for $250.
We find, therefore, that Appellant was not negligent in her operation of the
Government vehicle and that she is not liable, pursuant to 410 DM 114-60.808-4 (a),
for $250.
This decision constitutes the final administrative determination of the
Department in this matter. 43 C.F.R § 4.1(b)(4); 410 DM 114-60.808-7.
